subject: Does sampling time series' lag order make sense?

messages.author: df2011c04ce6269d
messages.subject: Does sampling time series' lag order make sense?
parts:
My original ARMA code treat lag-order d as a data input, sampling several models with different lag-order d and decide lag-order d by WAIC.
As I want to simplify how model choose lag-order, I modify and declare a real parameter which coresponds to a integer in model scope like below:

parameters {
  ...
  real<lower=1, upper=(T/ 10.0)> d2;  # T is length of time series
  ...
}

model {
   ...
    int d;
    d <- 1;
    while (d < d2) d <- d + 1;
   ...
}

Is there any paper support this?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Does sampling time series' lag order make sense?
parts:
I'm not sure how you could then code the rest of the model,
but it's not a good idea in Stan because your d2 will not
be sampled well because there is no gradient information (it
gets lost in the transform to d).

To build this in Stan, you want to create a mixture model of lags
1 to 10, then build up an array lp[10] where lp[d] is the
log density of the component for lag d. Then use

increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp));

There's a chapter in the manual on mixture models and another
on marginalizing discrete parameters that you may find helpful in
doing this.

The choice I see you facing is whether to tie the parameters
at lag d across d, d + 1, ..., 10 so that they're the same
for all mixture components. I would guess you would want
separate parameters, because that's closest to the model comparison
approach.

What we generally recommend in these situations is to just fit
the d == 10 case with priors on the lag components that will
shrink the effects toward zero if there is not enough data to
support them. It will be much more efficient (10 vs. 10^2 work
and probably an easier model to fit), and you can then just inspect
the parameters to see if there are effects at longer lags.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Does sampling time series' lag order make sense?
parts:
The model's maximum lag-order is not 10 and is depends on length of time series (T / 10.0). I originally use metaheuristic algorithm with WAIC as target function to determine lag-order, mixturing all models may exhausts computing power and memory.
keeping all lag components doesn't fit my need because some integer parameters are breaking point of time series.
I'm not familiar how NUTS sampler works but I think sampling may eliminates the use of metaheuristic algorithm.
Can NUTS sampler work even there is no gradient information? How bad would it be?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Does sampling time series' lag order make sense?
parts:
No, HMC won't work if there's no gradient information. There's no
guarantee you'll get the right distribution in the end if the
function's not differentiable on its support.

It'll work the same way whether you build the mixture as 1 to 10
or 1 to T/10 (don't do /10.0, or you'll get a floating point
number --- T/10 will round down).

But as I said before, I'd try just building one time series and
inspecting the parameters to judge how long-distance the effects
are.

- Bob
